bib.title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation", Sayash Kapoor*, Benedikt Stroebl* and 28 others, last author Arvind Narayanan. Preprint; the only venue marking is "arXiv:2510.11977v1 [cs.AI] 13 Oct 2025". No affiliations are printed: p1 says "Author affiliations and a link to our repository are available on hal.cs.princeton.edu", and the contact addresses are @princeton.edu.

COVERAGE: 66 of 66 pages, 174,213 chars. Read in full: body p1-10, appendices A1-A8 p17-36, A10 per-benchmark leaderboards p41-66. Skimmed: references p11-17 and Table A12 p37-40 (list of prior model-benchmark evaluations, no results). Chart-only pages yield axis ticks and legends, so per-point plot values were not readable; the tables were.

CLAIMS

1. Scale
   - number: 21,730 rollouts, 9 models, 9 benchmarks, about $40,000, 2.5B tokens of logs
   - setup: four domains (coding, web, science, customer service); prices as of 24 Sep 2025
   - quote: "21,730 agent rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks in coding, web navigation, science, and customer service with a total cost of about $40,000" (p1)
   - also: "We report 142 model-scaffold-benchmark combinations in our analysis (Section 4) from a total of 186 runs." (p22)

2. No repeated runs or confidence intervals for most results
   - quote: "For HAL, we were forced to rely on single runs without statistical validation for most evaluations." (p20, A3)
   - Appendix Pareto plots carry "Min-Max" bars, and leaderboard tables show "the accuracy of its best run" (p41). Which configurations had more than one run is not stated.

3. More reasoning effort did not help in most pairs
   - number: 21 of 36
   - setup: Opus 4.1, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 3.7 (none vs high, 4,096 thinking tokens) and o4-mini (low vs high), same scaffold and benchmark, single runs
   - quote: "in 21 of 36 model-agent-benchmark combinations, increased reasoning effort produces equal or lower accuracy" (p7)

4. The most expensive model is rarely on the cost-accuracy frontier
   - quote: "In only 1 of 9 benchmarks do we observe the most costly model run on the Pareto frontier." (p6)
   - quote: "less than one-third of tested models are on the frontier for a given benchmark. The three models most frequently on the Pareto frontier, Gemini 2.0 Flash (7 of 9 benchmarks), GPT-5 (4 of 9), and o4-mini Low (4 of 9)" (p6)
   - Opus 4.1 is on the dollar frontier once (CORE-Bench Hard) but on the token frontier in 3 of 8 benchmarks (p7).

5. Scaffold choice moves cost about 9x at near-equal accuracy
   - setup: Online Mind2Web, 300 tasks; Table A16 gives 42.3% vs 40.0%
   - quote: "SeeAct with GPT-5 Medium costs $171 while Browser-Use with Claude Sonnet 4 costs $1,577: a 9x difference in cost despite just a two-percentage-point difference in accuracy" (p7-8)

6. Task-specific scaffolds usually beat the generalist one
   - quote: "the task-specific CORE-Agent outperforms the generalist scaffold on 9 of 12 runs. A similar gap appears on SWE-bench Verified Mini (11 of 12). The generalist scaffolds also cost less in 20 of 24 model comparisons" (p8)

7. Benchmark cost varies widely
   - quote: "The cheapest benchmark, ScienceAgentBench, averages $13 per evaluation. The most expensive, Online Mind2Web, averages over $450." (p8)
   - Opus 4.1 was not run on Online Mind2Web, estimated at about $20,000.

8. Log inspection: method and validation
   - method: Docent (Meng et al., 2025) with GPT-5 Medium as judge; six rubrics (instruction violation, tool-use failure, self-correction, verification, environmental barrier, shortcuts/gaming), refined iteratively into natural-language decision trees
   - quote: "This sample comprises 48 distinct model-scaffold pairs and 2,184 transcripts. After removing TauBench ... 36 model-scaffold pairs and 1,634 transcripts." (p26)
   - validation (Table A2, p27): precision against human labels only, one rubric per benchmark. AssistantBench instruction following 0.87 (n=49, inter-LLM kappa 0.82 against Claude Sonnet 4); CORE-Bench verification 1.00 (n=31); TAU-bench instruction following 0.94 (n=36). No recall: "it is much easier to validate false positives than false negatives" (p26).

9. What the logs showed
   - Leakage: "the few-shot agent included in the official benchmark repository included actual benchmark examples in its few-shot data, constituting data leakage" (p9). Found after about $1,000 of runs; the scaffold was excluded (p23).
   - Shortcuts: "eight cases where agents found a gold answer, either by finding the answers of the dataset on HuggingFace or locating them on arXiv" (p9). Hard-coded values to pass tests on CORE-Bench and SciCode (Tables A7, A10).
   - Unsafe actions on TAU-bench: wrong credit card charged, $2,010 charged against a $1,000 budget (Table A6, p29).
   - Failures: instruction violation on failed tasks 0.670 (AssistantBench) and 0.628 (CORE-Bench); environmental barrier on failed tasks 0.564, 0.438, 0.403 (Table A3, p27).
   - Success correlates: relative success with self-correction 1.47, 1.54, 2.97; with verification 1.39, 1.87, 1.13 (Table A4, p27).
   - Harness conflict: AssistantBench's abstention instruction clashes with the Browser-Use scaffold's, so intended abstentions get graded as answers (p9, Table A9).

LIMITS
- Mostly single runs, so the 21-of-36 result and frontier membership have no noise estimate.
- Small subsets: SWE-bench Verified Mini 50 tasks, TAU-bench Airline 50, AssistantBench 33 of 214, CORE-Bench Hard 45, GAIA public validation 165.
- The log findings are correlations. Authors: "we cannot determine whether addressing these failures would lead to successful task completion" (p22).
- No recall and no shortcut prevalence rate; the judge was validated on one rubric per benchmark.
- SWE-Agent costs ignore cache hits (overstated). Reasoning-effort levels are not comparable across providers. Latency is not reported.
- Unstated: the claim that task-specific scaffolds "consistently outperform" does not fit Table A15, where the generalist tops GAIA (64.8%) over HF Open Deep Research. GAIA generalist runs were left out of Section 4 as incomplete.
- Dated: September 2025 prices and model list.

BUILDS ON: Kapoor et al. 2025 (AI Agents That Matter, TMLR); Liang et al. 2023 (HELM); Biderman et al. 2024 (LM Evaluation Harness); Meng et al. 2025 (Docent); Zhu et al. 2025a (agentic benchmark best practices); Henderson et al. 2018; Agarwal et al. 2022; Wandb Weave 2024; LiteLLM 2025.

CODE: none beyond the scaffold contract, "a Python run(input, **kwargs) → dict function" (p20).

FIGURES: Figure 3, p6, "Effect of higher reasoning on accuracy". One bar per model-scaffold-benchmark pair, showing change in accuracy from higher reasoning, range about -30 to +30 points. It shows both the sign split and the spread at once. The note already carries a Pareto figure from the 2024 paper, so Figure 2 (p7) would repeat it.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- The abstract says higher reasoning effort was "reducing accuracy in the majority of runs"; the body and Figure 3 say "equal or lower" or "does not improve". Use the body wording.
- "9 models" in the headline, but the appendix leaderboards list 12 to 19 model configurations (including Sonnet 4, Opus 4, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview, DeepSeek V3.1).
- Section A7.2 says validation covered AssistantBench, CORE-Bench and SciCode; Table A2 lists TAU-bench, not SciCode.
- Table A4, SciCode self-correction: delta printed as 0.37, but 0.483 minus 0.314 is 0.17.
- The body says self-correction makes success "between 1.5x and 4x more likely"; the Table A4 maximum is 2.97.
- Of the "eight cases" of found gold answers, Table A8 shows three, and in two the agent did not use the answer.
- Figure 2 caption says Opus 4.1 is on the frontier "1 of 8"; the body says the most costly model is on it in "1 of 9".
